Joint World Action Models through
Differentiable Trajectory Optimization

Mintae Kim & Koushil Sreenath Affiliation: Hybrid Robotics, BAIR, UC Berkeley Affiliation: {mintae.kim, koushils}@berkeley.edu
Abstract

Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present world action trajectory optimization (WATO), which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across 77 visual control environments, WATO improves average success from 79.9%79.9\% for the imitation joint WAM to 91.7%91.7\%, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average 11.5×11.5\times faster and uses 600.5×600.5\times fewer world model evaluations at deployment.

1 Introduction

Generative policies learn distributions over actions or action trajectories from data, reducing online planning (Janner et al., 2022; Chi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2025b). Recent world action models (WAMs) connect action generation with future prediction (Zhu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). We focus on joint WAMs that generate future actions and states or observations together. We treat them as a model class over world-action trajectories, independent of architecture or scale. Unlike generative policies, joint WAMs specify both how the agent acts and where the trajectory is intended to go. This provides richer information for control, but does not make the trajectory task-effective.

A joint WAM trained by trajectory imitation mainly reproduces the offline data distribution. Its generated actions need not reach the goal, and its generated states need not match the consequences of those actions under the control dynamics. A trajectory can therefore be data-consistent yet task-ineffective or dynamics-inconsistent. The problem is not only to improve the actions, but to optimize the world-action trajectory as a whole. This leads to our central question:

How should joint world-action trajectories be optimized for task performance while remaining consistent with action-conditioned dynamics?

Several existing approaches provide natural alternatives, but each uses only part of the world-action trajectory. Model-based planners optimize actions through world model rollouts (Chua et al., 2018; Kim and Sreenath, 2026b), but omit generated future states and require online optimization. Task losses can be backpropagated through learned dynamics (Hafner et al., 2020), but supervise only the actions. Consistency objectives can align generated states with world model predictions (Huang et al., 2026), but use them as prediction targets rather than control references. Optimized trajectories can also be distilled into a policy (Pinneri et al., 2021), but detached targets discard how the solution depends on the generated trajectory. None of these approaches uses both generated actions and future states to parameterize trajectory optimization and learn through its optimized solution.

We introduce world action trajectory optimization (WATO). WATO uses generated actions and future states as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem. The WAM proposes an intended trajectory, while a world model predicts the consequences of its actions (Zhou et al., 2025a; Sobal et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026; Kim and Sreenath, 2026a). The task objective drives the trajectory toward the goal. The action reference specifies how to move, and the state reference specifies where to go. Trajectory optimization combines both references with the world model to produce a task-directed, dynamics-consistent trajectory.

The generated world-action trajectory does not only initialize the optimizer, but it also parameterizes the optimization objective. Changing either the actions or future states can therefore change the optimized trajectory. WATO differentiates the task loss through this solution using implicit differentiation (Amos et al., 2018; Wan et al., 2024), providing task gradients to both generated actions and states. Flow matching provides offline trajectory imitation (Lipman et al., 2023), while trajectory optimization makes the joint WAM task-aware.

Trajectory optimization is used only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate world-action trajectories and evaluates their action sequences with the world model, i.e. action-conditioned dynamics. Deployment performs a lightweight best-of-KK selection over these proposals, but no iterative trajectory optimization is required.

We evaluate WATO on 77 visual control environments spanning navigation, reaching, contact-rich manipulation, and multi-stage goal-conditioned control. WATO improves average success from 79.9%79.9\% for the imitation-trained joint WAM to 91.7%91.7\%, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with CEM, WATO is 11.5×11.5\times faster and uses 600.5×600.5\times fewer world model evaluations. We also show that differentiating through trajectory optimization outperforms direct rollout, consistency regularization, and distillation. Removing either the action or state reference reduces performance, showing that both are crucial for control.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We study joint WAMs as generative models over world-action trajectories and formulate task-aware world-action generation as dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization.

  • •

    We introduce WATO, which uses generated actions and future states as optimization references and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator.

  • •

    We show across diverse control tasks that WATO improves joint world-action generation, outperforms strong model-based and learning-based baselines, and amortizes trajectory optimization into the generator for efficient deployment.

2 Preliminaries

Visual offline goal-conditioned control. We consider a reward-free offline dataset of NN visual trajectories, 𝒟={τ(n)}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\{\tau^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}, where τ(n)=(o0(n),a0(n),…,oTn(n))\tau^{(n)}=(o_{0}^{(n)},a_{0}^{(n)},\ldots,o_{T_{n}}^{(n)}), with visual observations ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O} and primitive actions at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}. We group BB consecutive actions into an action block Ah=(at+h​B,…,at+(h+1)​B−1)∈𝒰A_{h}=(a_{t+hB},\ldots,a_{t+(h+1)B-1})\in\mathcal{U}, where 𝒰:=𝒜B\mathcal{U}:=\mathcal{A}^{B}. An action trajectory A=(A0,…,AH−1)∈𝒰HA=(A_{0},\ldots,A_{H-1})\in\mathcal{U}^{H} spans L=B​HL=BH environment steps.

We use pretrained latent world models following LeWM (Maes et al., 2026). The encoder maps an observation to a latent state zt=Eθ​(ot)z_{t}=E_{\theta}(o_{t}), and the action-conditioned predictor rolls out future latent states from an action trajectory. Given ztz_{t} and AA, we write

Z^​(A)=ℛθ​(zt,A)=(z^1,…,z^H).\hat{Z}(A)=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A)=(\hat{z}_{1},\ldots,\hat{z}_{H}). (1)

A goal observation ogo_{g} is encoded as g=Eθ​(og)g=E_{\theta}(o_{g}). For a latent trajectory Z=(z1,…,zH)Z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{H}), we use the terminal goal cost J⁡(Z,g)=‖zH−g‖22J(Z,g)=\|z_{H}-g\|_{2}^{2}. Control proceeds in receding horizon by repeatedly generating an action trajectory, executing a segment, and planning from the new observation.

Generative policies and joint WAMs. Let c=(zt,g)c=(z_{t},g) denote the context that includes the current-state and goal condition. An action-only generative policy models A~∼qϕA​(A∣c)\tilde{A}\sim q_{\phi}^{A}(A\mid c). We focus on joint WAMs, which instead model future actions and states together:

(A~,Z~)∼qϕ​(A,Z∣c),Z~=(z~1,…,z~H).(\tilde{A},\tilde{Z})\sim q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid c),\qquad\tilde{Z}=(\tilde{z}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{z}_{H}). (2)

A joint WAM therefore induces an action-only distribution through the marginal qϕ,A​(A∣c)=∫qϕ​(A,Z∣c)​𝑑Zq_{\phi,A}(A\mid c)=\int q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid c)\,dZ. The distinction is the generated object: an action-only policy generates how to act, while a joint WAM additionally generates an intended future trajectory.

The generated future Z~\tilde{Z} is distinct from the world model prediction Z^​(A~)=ℛθ​(zt,A~)\hat{Z}(\tilde{A})=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}). The joint WAM proposes both actions and future states, while the pretrained world model predicts the states induced by those actions. Throughout the paper, ⋅~\tilde{\cdot} denotes a generated proposal, ⋅^\hat{\cdot} a world model prediction, and ⋅⋆{\cdot}^{\star} an optimized trajectory.

We parameterize the joint WAM with conditional flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023). For data xx, noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), condition cc, and flow time s∼Unif⁡[0,1]s\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1], we use the linear path xs=(1−s)​ϵ+s​xx_{s}=(1-s)\epsilon+sx and train vϕ​(xs,s,c)v_{\phi}(x_{s},s;c) toward x−ϵx-\epsilon. Section 3 applies this objective to joint action-state trajectories and makes the resulting generator task-aware through trajectory optimization.

3 World Action Trajectory Optimization

3.1 Imitating World-Action Trajectories Is Not Enough

We first train a joint world action flow (WAF) to imitate state-action trajectories from the offline dataset. For a local trajectory, let X=(A,Z)X=(A,Z) and condition the generator on the current state and goal, c=(zt,g)c=(z_{t},g). For each training window, we use its final observation as the goal. The WAF generates actions and future states jointly as (A~,Z~)∼qϕ(A,Z∣zt,g)(\tilde{A},\tilde{Z})\sim q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid z_{t},g).

We parameterize qϕq_{\phi} with conditional flow matching. Let ϵ=(ϵA,ϵZ)∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon=(\epsilon_{A},\epsilon_{Z})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), s∼Unif⁡[0,1]s\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1], and Xs=(1−s)​ϵ+s​XX_{s}=(1-s)\epsilon+sX. The joint vector field vϕ=(vϕA,vϕZ)v_{\phi}=(v_{\phi}^{A},v_{\phi}^{Z}) is trained with

ℒWAF=𝔼⁡[MSE⁡(vϕA​(Xs,s,c),A−ϵA)+λWAF​MSE⁡(vϕZ​(Xs,s,c),Z−ϵZ)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WAF}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{MSE}\left(v_{\phi}^{A}(X_{s},s;c),A-\epsilon_{A}\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{WAF}}\operatorname{MSE}\left(v_{\phi}^{Z}(X_{s},s;c),Z-\epsilon_{Z}\right)\right]. (3)

This objective imitates the joint state-action distribution in the offline data, but does not optimize trajectories for control. The generated actions need not reach the goal under the pretrained dynamics, so J⁡(ℛθ​(zt,A~),g)J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}),g) can remain large. The generated states also need not match the consequences of those actions, so Z~\tilde{Z} need not equal ℛθ​(zt,A~)\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}). Imitation alone therefore provides neither task optimality nor per-sample dynamics-consistency.

3.2 Why Not Optimize the Generator Directly?

A simple way to provide task-awareness is to evaluate its generated actions through the world model. Direct rollout training minimizes ℒrollout=J⁡(ℛθ​(zt,A~),g)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rollout}}=J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}),g). This provides a task gradient to A~\tilde{A}, but Z~\tilde{Z} does not affect action optimization. The joint WAF is thus used only as an action generator.

A stronger variant can also match the generated states to the world model rollout. For example, one can minimize ℒdirect+cons=J⁡(ℛθ​(zt,A~),g)+β​dZ​(ℛθ​(zt,A~),Z~)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{direct+cons}}=J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}),g)+\beta d_{Z}(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}),\tilde{Z}). This encourages dynamics-consistency, but still trains Z~\tilde{Z} to follow the rollout rather than to guide trajectory optimization.

Another alternative is optimization distillation. Given a generated proposal τ~=(A~,Z~)\tilde{\tau}=(\tilde{A},\tilde{Z}), a trajectory optimizer produces an optimized trajectory τ⋆\tau^{\star}, which is then treated as a detached regression target. This transfers optimized trajectories to the generator, but discards how τ⋆\tau^{\star} changes with τ~\tilde{\tau}. The optimizer provides targets rather than gradients through the optimized solution.

These alternatives either leave the generated future outside trajectory optimization or use optimization only to produce detached targets. WATO instead uses the full generated state-action trajectory to define the optimization problem and learns through its optimized solution.

3.3 Dynamics-Constrained Trajectory Projection

WATO uses the generated trajectory as a reference for trajectory optimization rather than executing it directly. For the current state ztz_{t}, define the set of trajectories consistent with the pretrained world model as ℱθ(zt)={(A,Z):A∈𝒰H,Z=ℛθ(zt,A)}\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(z_{t})=\{(A,Z):A\in\mathcal{U}^{H},\,Z=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A)\}. Given a generated reference τ~=(A~,Z~)\tilde{\tau}=(\tilde{A},\tilde{Z}), we define the dynamics-constrained trajectory projection

Πθ,g​(τ~)=arg​min(A,Z)∈ℱθ​(zt)⁡J​(Z,g)+λA​dA​(A,A~)+λZ​dZ​(Z,Z~)\displaystyle\Pi_{\theta,g}(\tilde{\tau})=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{(A,Z)\in\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(z_{t})}J(Z,g)+\lambda_{A}d_{A}(A,\tilde{A})+\lambda_{Z}d_{Z}(Z,\tilde{Z}) (4)

The task cost drives the trajectory toward the goal. The action reference preserves how the WAM proposes to move, while the state reference preserves where it proposes to go. The world model constrains these references through action-conditioned dynamics.

We use dA​(A,A~)=H−1​∑h=0H−1‖Ah−A~h‖22d_{A}(A,\tilde{A})=H^{-1}\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\|A_{h}-\tilde{A}_{h}\|_{2}^{2} and dZ​(Z,Z~)=H−1​∑h=1H‖𝒩Z​(zh)−𝒩Z​(z~h)‖22d_{Z}(Z,\tilde{Z})=H^{-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\|\mathcal{N}_{Z}(z_{h})-\mathcal{N}_{Z}(\tilde{z}_{h})\|_{2}^{2}, where 𝒩Z\mathcal{N}_{Z} is a fixed latent standardization. We solve Equation 4 in reduced space, with the action trajectory as the only optimization variable and Z⁡(A)=ℛθ​(zt,A)Z(A)=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A). The optimization becomes

A⋆=arg​minA∈𝒰H⁡J​(Z⁡(A),g)+λA​dA​(A,A~)+λZ​dZ​(Z⁡(A),Z~),Z⋆=Z⁡(A⋆).A^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{A\in\mathcal{U}^{H}}J\!\left(Z(A),g\right)+\lambda_{A}d_{A}(A,\tilde{A})+\lambda_{Z}d_{Z}(Z(A),\tilde{Z}),\qquad Z^{\star}=Z(A^{\star}). (5)

The optimized trajectory is task-directed and dynamics-consistent while remaining close to the generated state-action trajectory. Importantly, Z~\tilde{Z} is a reference, not an independently optimized state trajectory. Dynamics-consistency follows from the world model rollout rather than an additional penalty. Because both A~\tilde{A} and Z~\tilde{Z} parameterize the optimization objective, changing either reference can change the optimized trajectory. We next characterize this dependence and show how generated future states shape action optimization through the learned dynamics.

3.4 Learning Through the Optimized Trajectory

The generated trajectory parameterizes the trajectory optimization problem, not only its initialization. Define the task objective F⁡(A)=J⁡(ℛθ​(zt,A),g)F(A)=J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A),g) and the standardized rollout r⁡(A)=vec⁡𝒩Z​(ℛθ​(zt,A))r(A)=\operatorname{vec}\mathcal{N}_{Z}(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A)). We similarly write r~=vec⁡𝒩Z​(Z~)\tilde{r}=\operatorname{vec}\mathcal{N}_{Z}(\tilde{Z}). The reduced objective in Equation 5 is Ψ⁡(A,A~,r~)=F⁡(A)+λA​H−1​‖A−A~‖22+λZ​H−1​‖r⁡(A)−r~‖22\Psi(A;\tilde{A},\tilde{r})=F(A)+\lambda_{A}H^{-1}\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{Z}H^{-1}\|r(A)-\tilde{r}\|_{2}^{2}.

Let S⋆=∂r⁡(A)/∂A|A=A⋆S_{\star}=\partial r(A)/\partial A|_{A=A^{\star}} denote the standardized world model rollout Jacobian. For an interior local solution, the first-order condition is

∇F​(A⋆)+2​λAH​(A⋆−A~)+2​λZH​S⋆⊤​(r⁡(A⋆)−r~)=0.\nabla F(A^{\star})+\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}(A^{\star}-\tilde{A})+\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}S_{\star}^{\top}\bigl(r(A^{\star})-\tilde{r}\bigr)=0. (6)

The action reference acts directly in action space. The state reference acts through S⋆⊤S_{\star}^{\top}, which maps a future-state error into an action-space optimization direction. Generated future states therefore affect trajectory optimization through the action-conditioned world dynamics.

Proposition 1 (Dynamics-aware reference sensitivity). Suppose A⋆A^{\star} is an interior local solution, Ψ\Psi is twice continuously differentiable near A⋆A^{\star}, and ℋ⋆:=∇A​A2​Ψ​(A⋆,A~,r~)\mathcal{H}_{\star}:=\nabla_{AA}^{2}\Psi(A^{\star};\tilde{A},\tilde{r}) is nonsingular. Then

∂A⋆∂A~=2​λAH​ℋ⋆−1,∂A⋆∂r~=2​λZH​ℋ⋆−1​S⋆⊤\displaystyle\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial\tilde{A}}=\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}\mathcal{H}_{\star}^{-1},\qquad\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial\tilde{r}}=\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}\mathcal{H}_{\star}^{-1}S_{\star}^{\top} (7)

Actions affect the optimized trajectory through the local optimization Hessian. Future states additionally pass through the rollout Jacobian, so their influence depends on how actions change the predicted future. Both references can thus receive task gradients through the optimized solution.

This structure also changes the local geometry of action optimization. The state-reference term contributes 2​S⋆⊤​S⋆2S_{\star}^{\top}S_{\star} plus a residual-weighted second-order term from the rollout. When the state-reference residual is small, the local Hessian is approximated by

ℋ⋆≈∇2F​(A⋆)+2​λAH​I+2​λZH​S⋆⊤​S⋆.\mathcal{H}_{\star}\approx\nabla^{2}F(A^{\star})+\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}I+\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}S_{\star}^{\top}S_{\star}. (8)

Corollary 1 (Dynamics-induced local geometry). The action reference contributes isotropic curvature in action space, while the state reference contributes the positive-semidefinite term S⋆⊤​S⋆S_{\star}^{\top}S_{\star}. Action perturbations are therefore weighted by how strongly they change the predicted future. Generated states thus shape the local geometry of trajectory optimization through the learned dynamics.

We compute these sensitivities by implicit differentiation of the trajectory optimality conditions. Further derivations and local analysis are given in Appendix C.

3.5 The WATO Objective

Let τ~ϕ=(A~,Z~)∼qϕ(A,Z∣zt,g)\tilde{\tau}_{\phi}=(\tilde{A},\tilde{Z})\sim q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid z_{t},g) denote a generated trajectory and τ⋆=(A⋆,Z⋆)=Πθ,g​(τ~ϕ)\tau^{\star}=(A^{\star},Z^{\star})=\Pi_{\theta,g}(\tilde{\tau}_{\phi}) its optimized trajectory. WATO trains the same joint WAF with both imitation and task supervision:

ℒWATO=ℒWAF+λtask​𝔼​[J⁡(Z⋆,g)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WATO}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WAF}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{task}}\mathbb{E}\left[J(Z^{\star},g)\right] (9)

The flow matching term continues to imitate offline state-action trajectories, while the task term favors generated references that lead to better optimized trajectories.

The task gradient passes through the optimized trajectory as

d​J​(Z⋆,g)d​ϕ=∂J∂τ⋆​∂τ⋆∂τ~ϕ⏟solution sensitivity​∂τ~ϕ∂ϕ.\frac{dJ(Z^{\star},g)}{d\phi}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial\tau^{\star}}\underbrace{{\color[rgb]{0.0781,0.2891,0.6484}\frac{\partial\tau^{\star}}{\partial\tilde{\tau}_{\phi}}}}_{\mathclap{\text{solution sensitivity}}}\frac{\partial\tilde{\tau}_{\phi}}{\partial\phi}. (10)

By Proposition 1, action gradients pass through the local optimization Hessian, while state gradients additionally pass through the rollout Jacobian. The world model is differentiable when computing these gradients, but its parameters θ\theta remain fixed. WATO updates only the generator parameters ϕ\phi.

3.6 Training and Deployment

WATO uses two training stages. We first pretrain the joint WAF with ℒWAF\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WAF}} to imitate offline state-action trajectories. We then continue training the same generator with ℒWATO\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WATO}}, differentiating through trajectory optimization to provide task supervision.

Trajectory optimization is removed after training. At deployment, WATO generates KK independent proposals (A~(k),Z~(k))∼qϕ(A,Z∣zt,g)(\tilde{A}^{(k)},\tilde{Z}^{(k)})\sim q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid z_{t},g). Each action proposal is rolled out with the pretrained world model as Z^(k)=ℛθ​(zt,A~(k))\hat{Z}^{(k)}=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}^{(k)}). The controller selects k⋆=arg​mink⁡J​(Z^(k),g)k^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{k}J(\hat{Z}^{(k)},g) and executes the selected action segment in receding horizon. The generated state trajectory is not directly scored at deployment. It contributes through joint generation and trajectory-optimization training.

Optimization is used to train the generator, not to operate the deployed controller. Deployment requires only trajectory generation and world model evaluation. Full algorithm is provided in Algorithm 1.

Remark: Optimization amortization.

Under local regularity assumptions, small projection residuals bound the task-cost gap between generated and optimized trajectories and the generated trajectory’s inconsistency with the world model (see Appendix C.4).

4 Related Work

Generative policies and WAMs.

Generative policies learn distributions over actions or trajectories with multimodality (Janner et al., 2022; Ajay et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Park et al., 2025b). WAMs extend action generation by jointly modeling future actions and states or observations (Zhu et al., 2025; Cen et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). Recent work also studies how generated futures should be used at inference time (Yuan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). WATO instead optimizes the generated world-action trajectory for control. Generated actions and future states jointly define a dynamics-constrained optimization problem, and the generator is trained through its solution.

World models and model-based planning.

World models learn action-conditioned dynamics and use predicted futures to evaluate and/or optimize actions (Hafner et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2024; Sobal et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026). Model-based planners commonly optimize action sequences online using sampling or gradient-based methods (Power and Berenson, 2022; Zhou et al., 2025b). WATO uses a pretrained world model to constrain trajectory optimization during training. Deployment only requires trajectory generation and world model evaluation, without online optimization.

Differentiable optimization and generative control.

Differentiable optimization exposes how an optimized trajectory changes with model, cost, or policy parameters (Amos et al., 2018; Amos and Yarats, 2020). Prior work uses this principle to train policies through optimization or predictive control (Xu and She, 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2024). Other methods combine generative models with trajectory optimization, model-based projections, or MPC (Römer et al., 2024; Mizuta and Leung, 2026; Idoko et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). WATO uses both actions and future states to define the optimization objective, then differentiates task performance through its solution. Thus, differentiable optimization serves as a learning mechanism for WAMs rather than refinement only.

Offline goal-conditioned control.

Offline goal-conditioned RL (GCRL) learns to reach goals from fixed trajectory data. Prior methods include goal-conditioned behavior cloning, value learning, quasimetric learning, and hierarchical RL (Ding et al., 2019; Kostrikov et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Park et al., 2025a). WATO addresses the same downstream goal-reaching problem from a different direction. It starts from a joint WAF and makes its trajectories task-aware using a world model and differentiable trajectory optimization. We compare against these methods as goal-conditioned control baselines.

5 Experiments

We evaluate WATO along four questions. First, does world-action trajectory optimization improve goal-conditioned control over model-based, generative, and RL methods? Second, is differentiating through trajectory optimization more effective than direct task training or optimization distillation? Third, do generated future states improve control beyond action generation alone? Finally, is trajectory optimization successfully transferred into the generator during training?

5.1 Experimental Setup

Environments.

We evaluate WATO on 77 environments covering distinct control challenges. TwoRooms tests visual navigation, Reacher tests continuous reaching, and PushT tests contact-rich pushing (Maes et al., 2026). We additionally use four visual manipulation tasks from OGBench: cube-{single, double}, scene-play, and puzzle-3x3 (Park et al., 2025a). Together, these environments cover navigation, reaching, manipulation, and multi-stage goal-conditioned control.

Evaluation.

We evaluate goal reaching from offline data. Each initial observation is paired with a goal observation L=25L=25 primitive steps later in a evaluation trajectory, and the controller receives a 5050-step execution budget. Unless otherwise stated, WATO generates K=8K=8 candidates using 88 flow integration steps (NFE =8=8) at deployment. Success rate is the primary metric. We also report final goal error, latency, and world model evaluations in the appendix.

Baselines.

We compare against three groups of methods. For goal-conditioned learning, we use GCBC (Ding et al., 2019), GCIVL (Kostrikov et al., 2022), GCIQL (Park et al., 2025a), and QRL (Wang et al., 2023). For generative control, we compare with an flow policy, a joint WAF trained only by flow matching, and generative predictive control (GPC) (Kurtz and Burdick, 2026), adapted to our offline setting. For model-based control, we use CEM (Maes et al., 2026) and gradient-based MPC. GPC, CEM, gradient-based MPC, and WATO use the same pretrained LeWM. Model-based planners also use the same task cost. All methods use the same data, goal distribution, and evaluation protocol. Training details are given in Appendix F.2.

5.2 How Good is WATO for Visual Offline Goal-Conditioned Control?

We first evaluate WATO across all 77 environments. Table 1 reports the success rates. WATO achieves the highest macro-average success of 91.7%91.7\% and is best or tied for best on six of 77 environments, while GPC performs best on Reacher.

Compared with the joint WAF, WATO improves average success from 79.9%79.9\% to 91.7%91.7\%. This 11.811.8 percentage points (pp) gain shows that trajectory imitation alone does not fully exploit the generated state-action trajectory. Optimizing it during training makes the generator more effective for control.

WATO also outperforms online model-based planning. CEM and gradient-based MPC optimize actions at deployment using the same world model, achieving average success rates of 65.0%65.0\% and 76.7%76.7\%, respectively. WATO uses optimization only during training and deploys the generator without online optimization. Its gains therefore come from improving the generator rather than additional extensive test-time search. Section 5.5 examines this transfer of optimization into the generator.

5.3 What Does WATO Generate?

Figure 2 separates single-step candidate quality from full closed-loop behavior. A good local proposal does not necessarily yield reliable control over repeated planning.

At one planning step, WATO generates only K=8K=8 concentrated, low-error candidates. CEM uses 300300 rollouts but produces a broader candidate set, while the flow policy includes several large-error proposals. GCIQL and GCBC provide only a single proposal without candidate selection. WATO therefore achieves high-quality candidates with little test-time search.

Across eight heterogeneous episodes, WATO succeeds in 8/88/8, compared with 7/87/8 for the joint WAF, 6/86/8 for CEM, and 5/85/8 for the flow policy. Relative to the joint WAF, WATO yields a tighter candidate distribution and more reliable closed-loop trajectories. CEM also shows that more online search does not necessarily improve reliability. GCBC further illustrates the gap between local proposal quality and closed-loop behavior: its proposal in Fig. 2(a) can lie near the goal, yet only 5/85/8 episodes succeed in Fig. 2(b). Overall, WATO combines sample-efficient candidate generation with stable repeated planning.

5.4 How Beneficial is Differentiation Through Trajectory Optimization?

We next ask whether WATO benefits specifically from differentiating through trajectory optimization. All variants use the same joint WAF, offline data, and world model. Only the training objective changes. Joint WAF uses flow matching alone. Direct rollout adds the goal-reaching loss through the world model rollout, supervising the generated actions. Direct rollout + consistency also matches states to the rollout. Distillation trains the generator toward detached trajectories produced by the same optimizer. WATO instead differentiates through the optimized solution, allowing both action and state references to receive gradients according to how they affect that solution.

Figure 3 shows a steady improvement across these objectives. Joint WAF achieves 79.9%79.9\%, direct rollout 85.7%85.7\%, direct rollout with consistency 87.4%87.4\%, and distillation 88.0%88.0\%. WATO reaches 91.7%91.7\%, indicating that differentiating through optimization provides more effective supervision than direct task losses, consistency regularization, or detached optimized targets.

5.5 Is Trajectory Optimization Well-Amortized through WATO?

WATO uses trajectory optimization during training but removes it at deployment. We test whether this optimization is transferred into the generator by applying the same trajectory optimization layer before and after WATO training.

Table 5.5 reports the additional success obtained from online trajectory optimization. Before WATO training, optimization improves success by 10.410.4 pp on average. After WATO training, the remaining gain drops to 1.31.3 pp. Thus, WATO learns to generate goal-reaching and dynamics-consistent trajectories that already capture most of the benefit of trajectory optimization.

5.6 Should We Generate Both States and Actions?

We next isolate the roles of generated actions and future states. The action-only variant removes dZd_{Z}, while the state-only variant removes dAd_{A}. They achieve average success rates of 85.7%85.7\% and 85.0%85.0\%, respectively, compared with 91.7%91.7\% for full WATO. Thus, neither reference alone recovers the performance of their combination. Generated future states therefore contribute directly to trajectory optimization rather than serving only as auxiliary predictions. This result is consistent with Proposition 1: state references influence optimized actions through the world model rollout Jacobian. We further compare generated and rollout-derived state references to test whether generated futures provide benefits beyond dynamics-aware regularization (Appendix G.1).

5.7 How Does Trajectory Optimization Shape the Generator?

We next examine how the generator changes during WATO training on three environments: PushT, cube-double, and scene-play. For each generated world-action trajectory, we measure dA​(A⋆,A~)d_{A}(A^{\star},\tilde{A}), dZ​(Z⋆,Z~)d_{Z}(Z^{\star},\tilde{Z}), and the task improvement Δ​J=J⁡(ℛθ​(zt,A~),g)−J⁡(Z⋆,g)\Delta J=J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}),g)-J(Z^{\star},g) (see Sec. 3.3 for definitions).

Figure 4 shows that all three metrics decrease despite some fluctuations. From initialization to 1010k WATO steps, the action-reference distance decreases by 39.3%39.3\% on average across the three environments, the state-reference distance by 30.5%30.5\%, and the remaining goal-reaching task improvement by 31.8%31.8\%. The generator therefore moves closer to its optimized trajectories while requiring progressively less correction from trajectory optimization. This provides direct evidence that trajectory optimization is amortized into world-action generation.

5.8 How Efficient is WATO at Deployment?

Table 3 compares WATO with CEM at deployment. WATO reduces latency in every environment, with speedups from 5.8×5.8\times to 25.0×25.0\times and a geometric mean of 11.5×11.5\times. World model evaluations decrease more sharply, from 375×375\times to 1125×1125\times, with a geometric mean of 600.5×600.5\times.

The larger reduction in world model evaluations than in latency shows that model evaluations alone do not determine wall-clock time, because trajectory generation and execution remain. WATO and the joint WAF use the same deployment procedure, so WATO’s control gains require no additional test-time computation. Absolute latency, evaluation counts, and timing details are reported in Appendix H.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

WATO shows that trajectory optimization can train joint WAMs rather than only refine actions at deployment. Across 77 environments, it improves average success from 79.9%79.9\% for the joint WAF to 91.7%91.7\%, with ablations showing that both action and state references contribute. Decreasing projection residuals and optimization benefit further indicate that WATO transfers trajectory optimization into the generator. Generated future states also play a direct control role: as trajectory references, they shape optimized actions through the world model dynamics.

World models and joint WAMs therefore play complementary roles. The joint WAM proposes trajectories, while the pretrained world model provides action-conditioned dynamics during training and evaluates actions at deployment. WATO uses this model to improve generation without iterative online planning. Limitations include dependence on learned dynamics, the finite-horizon goal-conditioned setting, and evaluation only with flow matching. Extending WATO to robust longer-horizon control and other joint generative models remains open.
