Appendix A World Action Models as a Generative Control Model Class

We make this perspective manifest by treating WAMs as a mathematical class of conditional trajectory models, independent of architecture or scale. Let c=(zt,g)c=(z_{t},g) denote the current-state and goal condition. An action-only generative policy models qϕA​(A∣c)q_{\phi}^{A}(A\mid c), a world model represents action-conditioned dynamics pθ​(Z∣A,c)p_{\theta}(Z\mid A,c), and a joint WAM models qϕ​(A,Z∣c)q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid c). What differs is the modeled object. A joint WAM generates both an action trajectory and an intended future trajectory, with action marginal qϕ,A​(A∣c)=∫qϕ​(A,Z∣c)​𝑑Zq_{\phi,A}(A\mid c)=\int q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid c)\,dZ.

Model class and scale are separate choices.

A joint WAM does not require a particular architecture, generative parameterization, dataset scale, or pretraining regime. Autoregressive, diffusion, and flow-based models can all represent distributions over world-action trajectories. A joint WAM can likewise be task-specific or pretrained on heterogeneous data. Recent WAMs emphasize large-scale pretraining and generalization (Zhu et al., 2025; Cen et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). Here, we focus on the control problem that comes with generating a joint trajectory.

Joint generation exposes an additional control reference.

An action-only generator gives downstream control only an action trajectory. A joint WAM also provides a future trajectory Z~\tilde{Z}. For this extra output to matter for control, it should affect the resulting actions rather than act only as an auxiliary prediction. WATO uses A~\tilde{A} and Z~\tilde{Z} as references in the trajectory projection Πθ,g\Pi_{\theta,g}, so both can shape the optimized action trajectory. Proposition 1 in Sec. 3.4 makes this explicit: the state reference acts through the world model rollout Jacobian.

Scaling does not affect the control objective.

Learning a broad trajectory distribution and choosing good behavior for a downstream task are different problems. A large joint WAM may represent diverse behaviors and futures, but imitation alone does not ensure that a generated trajectory minimizes the task objective or matches the dynamics used for control. Pretraining determines what trajectory distribution the model represents. WATO shapes how that distribution is used for control.

The formulation is independent of the generator parameterization.

Our implementation uses flow matching, but WATO is defined at the level of generated world-action trajectories. The operator Πθ,g​(A~,Z~)\Pi_{\theta,g}(\tilde{A},\tilde{Z}) depends on action and state references and differentiable action-conditioned dynamics, not on the flow architecture itself. The same idea may therefore extend to other differentiable joint generative models, including larger pretrained WAMs. We leave this direction to future work.

Appendix B Why WATO Should Be Your Favorite Controller

Our results suggest WATO as a default controller for visual offline goal-conditioned control with local goals or waypoints. This raises a broader question: why does WATO also outperform value-based GCRL methods designed for long-horizon goal reaching? We look at local versus long-horizon control, representation, candidate selection, and the way each method learns a controller.

Short horizons do not make policy learning trivial.

OGBench uses goal relabeling during training and predefined start-goal tasks for evaluation (Park et al., 2025a). Our evaluation instead samples goals 2525 steps ahead in test trajectories and allows 5050 execution steps. Each pair has an observed local connection, so little cross-trajectory stitching is needed. But the controller still needs accurate contact, pose control, and recovery from execution errors. Being able to propagate goal-reaching values over long horizons does not automatically give a strong local controller.

The gap is not explained by the encoder alone.

The main comparisons use the same pretrained LeWM encoder to control for representation quality. End-to-end training with the official IMPALA-based setup raises GCIQL’s average success from 50.9%50.9\% to 53.9%53.9\%, with larger gains on scene-play and puzzle-3x3. So encoder training can help GCIQL, but it does not close the gap.

The advantage persists without candidate selection.

WATO with K=1K=1 achieves 88.7%88.7\% average success and outperforms both GCIQL variants in all 77 environments. Increasing KK to 88 adds another 3.03.0 percentage points. With K=1K=1, world model ranking cannot change the executed proposal, so best-of-KK selection alone cannot explain the advantage. Table 4 summarizes both controls.

Trajectory supervision directly matches the local control problem.

Each training window gives a current state, an attained future goal, and the actions and states in between. Goal-conditioned imitation uses the same kind of hindsight supervision (Ghosh et al., 2021), and GCRL also uses relabeled goals and dataset actions. So the key difference is not whether the methods see goal-reaching trajectories, but how they use them. GCIQL learns goal-conditioned values and extracts a policy using those values and a behavioral constraint (Park et al., 2025a). WATO instead learns the joint trajectory and sends task gradients through its optimized solution. In this sense, it trades bootstrapped value learning for model-based trajectory supervision while keeping the imitation signal.

Simply matching the goal distribution throughout trajectories is not enough. GCBC and the flow policy achieve 66.4%66.4\% and 69.3%69.3\% average success, compared with 79.9%79.9\% for Joint WAF and 91.7%91.7\% for WATO. Neither hindsight imitation nor action-only generation reaches the performance of WATO.

One trajectory sample can still represent coordinated behavior.

Reducing KK removes best-of-KK selection, but not the structure within a sampled trajectory. A joint WAF can generate an action sequence whose approach, contact, and subsequent motion follow one behavioral mode. This may help compared with extracting individual actions from a unimodal policy, becasue the continuous-action OGBench baselines use Gaussian policies evaluated at their means (Park et al., 2025a). Still, our comparisons do not cleanly separate temporal coordination, policy expressiveness, and the training objective. We therefore view trajectory generation as a useful inductive bias, not as something a Markov policy could never represent.

Lower GCRL performance does not point to value error alone.

The bottleneck could lie in value estimation, policy extraction, or generalization to states encountered during execution. Prior work shows that policy extraction and test-time generalization can limit offline RL even when value learning works well (Park et al., 2024). Our controls do not isolate these factors one by one, but they show that neither encoder choice nor best-of-KK selection explains the gap.

WATO takes a different route: it gets continuous task supervision through a learned rollout and trajectory optimization. This still depends on world model accuracy and on transferring optimized behavior into the unprojected generator, as analyzed in Appendix C.4.

WATO as the default local controller.

Taken together, our results point to a simple default: if the goal is to turn visual offline trajectories into a goal-conditioned controller, start with a joint WAM and optimize it for control. WATO outperforms the evaluated GCRL methods even when GCIQL trains its visual encoder end-to-end, and K=1K=1 WATO remains far ahead without best-of-KK selection. The gap is therefore not explained by representation quality or test-time candidate selection alone. WATO also keeps the resulting controller simple at deployment, requiring only trajectory generation and a small number of world model evaluations.

This does not make WAMs and GCRL mutually exclusive. Generative policies can be combined with value learning (Park et al., 2025b), and values may be useful when the problem requires trajectory stitching or reasoning far beyond locally supported trajectories. But that is a different job from learning a strong local controller. For the controller itself, our results give a clear answer: directly learn the trajectory, optimize it for the task, and amortize that optimization into the generator.

For visual offline goal-conditioned control, WATO should be your favorite controller.

Appendix C Theory and Derivations

This section develops the reference sensitivities and local geometry used in Sec. 3.4. We also study the local stability of the trajectory projection and connect its residuals to optimization amortization. All results are local, since the world model rollout and trajectory optimization problem are generally nonlinear and nonconvex.

C.1 Reference Sensitivity

We start from the reduced WATO objective

Ψ⁡(A,A~,r~)=F⁡(A)+λAH​‖A−A~‖22+λZH​‖r⁡(A)−r~‖22,\Psi(A;\tilde{A},\tilde{r})=F(A)+\frac{\lambda_{A}}{H}\|A-\tilde{A}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{\lambda_{Z}}{H}\|r(A)-\tilde{r}\|_{2}^{2}, (11)

where F⁡(A)=J⁡(ℛθ​(zt,A),g)F(A)=J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A),g), r⁡(A)=vec⁡𝒩Z​(ℛθ​(zt,A))r(A)=\operatorname{vec}\mathcal{N}_{Z}(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A)), and r~=vec⁡𝒩Z​(Z~)\tilde{r}=\operatorname{vec}\mathcal{N}_{Z}(\tilde{Z}). Let S⁡(A)=∂r⁡(A)/∂AS(A)=\partial r(A)/\partial A and write the first-order condition as

G⁡(A,A~,r~):=∇AΨ​(A,A~,r~)=0.G(A;\tilde{A},\tilde{r}):=\nabla_{A}\Psi(A;\tilde{A},\tilde{r})=0. (12)

For an interior local solution A⋆A^{\star}, this becomes

∇F​(A⋆)+2​λAH​(A⋆−A~)+2​λZH​S⋆⊤​(r⁡(A⋆)−r~)=0,\nabla F(A^{\star})+\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}(A^{\star}-\tilde{A})+\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}S_{\star}^{\top}\bigl(r(A^{\star})-\tilde{r}\bigr)=0, (13)

where S⋆=S⁡(A⋆)S_{\star}=S(A^{\star}). Let ℋ⋆=∇A​A2​Ψ​(A⋆,A~,r~)\mathcal{H}_{\star}=\nabla_{AA}^{2}\Psi(A^{\star};\tilde{A},\tilde{r}). If ℋ⋆\mathcal{H}_{\star} is nonsingular, the implicit function theorem gives

∂A⋆∂y=−ℋ⋆−1​∂G∂y,y∈{A~,r~}.\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial y}=-\mathcal{H}_{\star}^{-1}\frac{\partial G}{\partial y},\qquad y\in\{\tilde{A},\tilde{r}\}. (14)

The action reference enters Equation 13 directly, with ∂G/∂A~=−(2​λA/H)​I\partial G/\partial\tilde{A}=-(2\lambda_{A}/H)I. This gives

∂A⋆∂A~=2​λAH​ℋ⋆−1.\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial\tilde{A}}=\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}\mathcal{H}_{\star}^{-1}. (15)

The state reference enters through the world model rollout. Since ∂G/∂r~=−(2​λZ/H)​S⋆⊤\partial G/\partial\tilde{r}=-(2\lambda_{Z}/H)S_{\star}^{\top}, we get

∂A⋆∂r~=2​λZH​ℋ⋆−1​S⋆⊤.\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial\tilde{r}}=\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}\mathcal{H}_{\star}^{-1}S_{\star}^{\top}. (16)

Together, Equation 15-Equation 16 give Proposition 1. The action reference changes the optimized action trajectory through the local optimization Hessian, while the state reference additionally passes through S⋆⊤S_{\star}^{\top}, which maps changes in the predicted future back to action space. For box-constrained solutions, the same derivation applies locally on the free action coordinates when the active set is fixed.

C.2 Local Optimization Geometry

The Hessian of Equation 11 also shows how the two references shape the local optimization geometry. Define the state-reference residual e⁡(A)=r⁡(A)−r~e(A)=r(A)-\tilde{r}. Holding r~\tilde{r} fixed, its squared norm has gradient

∇A‖e⁡(A)‖22=2​S​(A)⊤​e​(A).\nabla_{A}\|e(A)\|_{2}^{2}=2S(A)^{\top}e(A). (17)

Writing ri​(A)r_{i}(A) and ei​(A)e_{i}(A) for the corresponding coordinates and differentiating again gives

∇A2‖e⁡(A)‖22=2​S​(A)⊤​S​(A)+2​∑iei​(A)​∇A2ri​(A).\nabla_{A}^{2}\|e(A)\|_{2}^{2}=2S(A)^{\top}S(A)+2\sum_{i}e_{i}(A)\nabla_{A}^{2}r_{i}(A). (18)

The exact Hessian at A⋆A^{\star} is

ℋ⋆=∇2F​(A⋆)+2​λAH​I+2​λZH​[S⋆⊤​S⋆+∑ie⋆,i​∇A2ri​(A⋆)],\mathcal{H}_{\star}=\nabla^{2}F(A^{\star})+\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}I+\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}\left[S_{\star}^{\top}S_{\star}+\sum_{i}e_{\star,i}\nabla_{A}^{2}r_{i}(A^{\star})\right], (19)

where e⋆=r⁡(A⋆)−r~e_{\star}=r(A^{\star})-\tilde{r}.

Approximating the state-reference Hessian by its Gauss-Newton term gives

ℋ⋆≈∇2F​(A⋆)+2​λAH​I+2​λZH​S⋆⊤​S⋆.\mathcal{H}_{\star}\approx\nabla^{2}F(A^{\star})+\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}I+\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}S_{\star}^{\top}S_{\star}. (20)

The task Hessian ∇2F​(A⋆)\nabla^{2}F(A^{\star}) is kept exact. If ‖∇A2​ri​(A)‖≤Mr\|\nabla_{A}^{2}r_{i}(A)\|\leq M_{r} for every coordinate in a neighborhood of A⋆A^{\star}, the omitted term satisfies

‖2​λZH​∑ie⋆,i​∇A2ri​(A⋆)‖≤2​λZ​MrH​‖e⋆‖1.\left\|\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}\sum_{i}e_{\star,i}\nabla_{A}^{2}r_{i}(A^{\star})\right\|\leq\frac{2\lambda_{Z}M_{r}}{H}\|e_{\star}\|_{1}. (21)

So the approximation error vanishes with the state-reference residual.

The action reference contributes isotropic curvature (2​λA/H)​I(2\lambda_{A}/H)I. The state-reference Gauss-Newton term is positive semidefinite since, for any action perturbation uu,

u⊤​S⋆⊤​S⋆​u=‖S⋆​u‖22≥0.u^{\top}S_{\star}^{\top}S_{\star}u=\|S_{\star}u\|_{2}^{2}\geq 0. (22)

It weights action directions by how strongly they change the standardized predicted trajectory. The task Hessian and residual-weighted term may still be indefinite, so this does not make the full objective convex.

Generated versus rollout-derived references.

One interesting distinction is that this geometry does not require a WAM-generated future. For a fixed proposal A~\tilde{A}, replacing r~\tilde{r} with r⁡(A~)r(\tilde{A}) gives the state-reference penalty λZ​H−1​‖r⁡(A)−r⁡(A~)‖22\lambda_{Z}H^{-1}\|r(A)-r(\tilde{A})\|_{2}^{2}. At the same action trajectory AA, its Gauss-Newton contribution is still (2​λZ/H)​S​(A)⊤​S​(A)(2\lambda_{Z}/H)S(A)^{\top}S(A). What changes is the reference itself, and hence the gradient, residual-weighted Hessian term, and optimized solution. Removing dZd_{Z} therefore tests the state-reference penalty as a whole, but does not separate generated-future information from dynamics-aware regularization. This motivates the generated versus rollout-derived reference comparison in Appendix G.1.

C.3 Projection Stability

The same sensitivity expressions also tell us how stable the projection is locally. Assume that Ψ\Psi is locally μ\mu-strongly convex in AA around A⋆A^{\star}, so that

ℋ⋆⪰μ​I,μ>0.\mathcal{H}_{\star}\succeq\mu I,\qquad\mu>0. (23)

Then ‖ℋ⋆−1‖≤1/μ\|\mathcal{H}_{\star}^{-1}\|\leq 1/\mu. Using Equation 15,

‖∂A⋆∂A~‖≤2​λAH​μ.\left\|\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial\tilde{A}}\right\|\leq\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H\mu}. (24)

Similarly,

‖∂A⋆∂r~‖≤2​λZH​μ​‖S⋆‖.\left\|\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial\tilde{r}}\right\|\leq\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H\mu}\|S_{\star}\|. (25)

For sufficiently small perturbations (Δ​A~,Δ​r~)(\Delta\tilde{A},\Delta\tilde{r}), these bounds give

‖Δ​A⋆‖≤2H​μ​(λA​‖Δ​A~‖+λZ​‖S⋆‖​‖Δ​r~‖)+o⁡(‖(Δ​A~,Δ​r~)‖).\|\Delta A^{\star}\|\leq\frac{2}{H\mu}\left(\lambda_{A}\|\Delta\tilde{A}\|+\lambda_{Z}\|S_{\star}\|\|\Delta\tilde{r}\|\right)+o(\|(\Delta\tilde{A},\Delta\tilde{r})\|). (26)

The action-reference sensitivity is controlled by the local curvature of the optimization problem. For the state reference, the rollout Jacobian also matters: it has more influence in directions where small action changes produce larger changes in the future.

C.4 Optimization Amortization

There is one subtlety in WATO: training evaluates the projected task cost F⁡(A⋆)F(A^{\star}), while deployment uses the unprojected proposal A~\tilde{A}. A good projected trajectory does not automatically imply a good raw proposal. For example, consider H=1H=1, r⁡(A)=Ar(A)=A, F⁡(A)=A2F(A)=A^{2}, and λA=λZ=1\lambda_{A}=\lambda_{Z}=1. The projection is

A⋆=arg​minA⁡[A2+(A−A~)2+(A−r~)2]=A~+r~3.A^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{A}\left[A^{2}+(A-\tilde{A})^{2}+(A-\tilde{r})^{2}\right]=\frac{\tilde{A}+\tilde{r}}{3}. (27)

Setting A~=t\tilde{A}=t and r~=−t\tilde{r}=-t gives F⁡(A⋆)=0F(A^{\star})=0 but F⁡(A~)=t2F(\tilde{A})=t^{2}. This example only concerns the projected task term. WATO still keeps trajectory imitation through ℒWAF\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WAF}}. The useful question is therefore when a small projection residual is enough to transfer the optimized behavior back to the raw proposal.

Residual-based deployment bounds.

For brevity, write dA=dA​(A⋆,A~)d_{A}=d_{A}(A^{\star},\tilde{A}) and dZ=dZ​(Z⋆,Z~)d_{Z}=d_{Z}(Z^{\star},\tilde{Z}), where Z⋆=ℛθ​(zt,A⋆)Z^{\star}=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A^{\star}). By definition,

‖A⋆−A~‖2=H​dA,‖r⁡(A⋆)−r~‖2=H​dZ.\|A^{\star}-\tilde{A}\|_{2}=\sqrt{Hd_{A}},\qquad\|r(A^{\star})-\tilde{r}\|_{2}=\sqrt{Hd_{Z}}. (28)

Suppose A⋆A^{\star} is an exact interior local solution. Assume that ∇F\nabla F is LFL_{F}-Lipschitz and rr is LrL_{r}-Lipschitz on a neighborhood containing the segment between A⋆A^{\star} and A~\tilde{A}. Below, matrix norms are spectral norms.

Residual-based deployment transfer.

The task-cost gap satisfies |F⁡(A~)−F⁡(A⋆)|≤(2​λA+H​LF2)​dA+2​λZ​‖S⋆‖​dA​dZ.\left|F(\tilde{A})-F(A^{\star})\right|\leq\left(2\lambda_{A}+\frac{HL_{F}}{2}\right)d_{A}+2\lambda_{Z}\|S_{\star}\|\sqrt{d_{A}d_{Z}}. (29) The inconsistency between the generated future and the rollout of the generated actions satisfies dZ​(ℛθ​(zt,A~),Z~)≤Lr​dA+dZ.\sqrt{d_{Z}\!\left(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}),\tilde{Z}\right)}\leq L_{r}\sqrt{d_{A}}+\sqrt{d_{Z}}. (30)

Proof. The first-order condition in Equation 13 gives

‖∇F​(A⋆)‖2≤2H​(λA​dA+λZ​‖S⋆‖​dZ).\|\nabla F(A^{\star})\|_{2}\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{H}}\left(\lambda_{A}\sqrt{d_{A}}+\lambda_{Z}\|S_{\star}\|\sqrt{d_{Z}}\right). (31)

Lipschitz continuity of ∇F\nabla F gives

|F⁡(A~)−F⁡(A⋆)|≤‖∇F​(A⋆)‖2​H​dA+H​LF2​dA.\left|F(\tilde{A})-F(A^{\star})\right|\leq\|\nabla F(A^{\star})\|_{2}\sqrt{Hd_{A}}+\frac{HL_{F}}{2}d_{A}. (32)

Substituting Equation 31 proves Equation 29. For the consistency bound, the triangle inequality gives

‖r⁡(A~)−r~‖2≤Lr​‖A~−A⋆‖2+‖r⁡(A⋆)−r~‖2.\|r(\tilde{A})-\tilde{r}\|_{2}\leq L_{r}\|\tilde{A}-A^{\star}\|_{2}+\|r(A^{\star})-\tilde{r}\|_{2}. (33)

Dividing by H\sqrt{H} gives Equation 30.

These bounds connect the reference distances in Figure 4 to two deployment quantities: the cost of removing optimization and the world model inconsistency of the generated trajectory. The second statement is with respect to the pretrained world model, not the true environment.

Stationarity and fixed points.

Under the same assumptions,

‖∇F​(A~)‖2≤2H​[(λA+H​LF2)​dA+λZ​‖S⋆‖​dZ].\|\nabla F(\tilde{A})\|_{2}\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{H}}\left[\left(\lambda_{A}+\frac{HL_{F}}{2}\right)\sqrt{d_{A}}+\lambda_{Z}\|S_{\star}\|\sqrt{d_{Z}}\right]. (34)

This follows from ‖∇F​(A~)‖2≤‖∇F​(A⋆)‖2+LF​‖A~−A⋆‖2\|\nabla F(\tilde{A})\|_{2}\leq\|\nabla F(A^{\star})\|_{2}+L_{F}\|\tilde{A}-A^{\star}\|_{2} and Equation 31. So small residuals also bound the task gradient of the raw proposal.

If A⋆=A~A^{\star}=\tilde{A} and r~=r⁡(A~)\tilde{r}=r(\tilde{A}), both distances vanish and

∇AJ​(ℛθ​(zt,A~),g)=0.\nabla_{A}J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}),g)=0. (35)

An interior dynamics-consistent fixed point is task-stationary and not necessarily globally optimal.

Active action bounds.

When action bounds are active, the full task gradient need not vanish. Let N𝒰H​(A)N_{\mathcal{U}^{H}}(A) denote the normal cone of the action box. Constrained optimality gives 0∈∇AΨ​(A⋆,A~,r~)+N𝒰H​(A⋆)0\in\nabla_{A}\Psi(A^{\star};\tilde{A},\tilde{r})+N_{\mathcal{U}^{H}}(A^{\star}), which implies

dist⁡(0,∇F​(A⋆)+N𝒰H​(A⋆))≤2H​(λA​dA+λZ​‖S⋆‖​dZ).\operatorname{dist}\left(0,\,\nabla F(A^{\star})+N_{\mathcal{U}^{H}}(A^{\star})\right)\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{H}}\left(\lambda_{A}\sqrt{d_{A}}+\lambda_{Z}\|S_{\star}\|\sqrt{d_{Z}}\right). (36)

At a dynamics-consistent fixed point, this becomes constrained task stationarity.

For feasible A~\tilde{A} and A⋆A^{\star} in a neighborhood where FF is CFC_{F}-Lipschitz, we can still bound the task-cost gap without assuming interior stationarity:

|F⁡(A~)−F⁡(A⋆)|≤CF​H​dA.\left|F(\tilde{A})-F(A^{\star})\right|\leq C_{F}\sqrt{Hd_{A}}. (37)

The dynamics-consistency bound in Equation 30 also continues to hold at active bounds, since its proof does not use stationarity.

Inexact optimization.

The same picture extends to approximate solves. For an approximate interior solution, let ϵopt=‖∇AΨ​(A⋆,A~,r~)‖2\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}=\|\nabla_{A}\Psi(A^{\star};\tilde{A},\tilde{r})\|_{2}, with all distances and Jacobians evaluated at the returned trajectory. The right-hand sides of Equations 31 and 34 then gain ϵopt\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}, while Equation 29 gains ϵopt​H​dA\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}\sqrt{Hd_{A}}. For a bound-active solution, Equation 36 similarly gains the corresponding KKT residual dist⁡(0,∇AΨ​(A⋆,A~,r~)+N𝒰H​(A⋆))\operatorname{dist}(0,\nabla_{A}\Psi(A^{\star};\tilde{A},\tilde{r})+N_{\mathcal{U}^{H}}(A^{\star})). The consistency and Lipschitz cost bounds do not require a converged projection.

Candidate selection under model error.

Finally, consider the deployed best-of-KK rule. For KK generated candidates and their projected trajectories, let k⋆=arg​mink⁡F​(A~(k))k^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{k}F(\tilde{A}^{(k)}). Let Fenv​(A)F_{\mathrm{env}}(A) denote the terminal task cost obtained by executing AA in the environment, using the same encoder and goal. Suppose |Fenv​(A)−F⁡(A)|≤ϵmodel|F_{\mathrm{env}}(A)-F(A)|\leq\epsilon_{\mathrm{model}} for every generated and projected action trajectory in this candidate set. Let ηk≥0\eta_{k}\geq 0 satisfy F⁡(A~(k))≤F⁡(A⋆(k))+ηkF(\tilde{A}^{(k)})\leq F(A^{\star(k)})+\eta_{k}, as provided by the preceding task-cost bounds. Then

Fenv​(A~(k⋆))\displaystyle F_{\mathrm{env}}(\tilde{A}^{(k^{\star})}) ≤mink⁡[Fenv​(A⋆(k))+ηk]+2​ϵmodel\displaystyle\leq\min_{k}\left[F_{\mathrm{env}}(A^{\star(k)})+\eta_{k}\right]+2\epsilon_{\mathrm{model}} (38)
≤mink⁡Fenv​(A⋆(k))+maxk⁡ηk+2​ϵmodel.\displaystyle\leq\min_{k}F_{\mathrm{env}}(A^{\star(k)})+\max_{k}\eta_{k}+2\epsilon_{\mathrm{model}}.

This follows from F⁡(A~(k⋆))≤F⁡(A~(k))≤F⁡(A⋆(k))+ηkF(\tilde{A}^{(k^{\star})})\leq F(\tilde{A}^{(k)})\leq F(A^{\star(k)})+\eta_{k} and the model-error bound on the selected and projected trajectories. The bound separates three effects: projected candidate quality, the cost of removing optimization, and world model error.

These results describe what small projection residuals buy us: WATO does not explicitly minimize them. They are finite-horizon statements and do not imply convergence of WATO training, closed-loop stability, or environment-defined success.

Appendix D Trajectory Optimization and Differentiation

WATO optimizes only the action trajectory and obtains future states from the world model rollout. The world model parameters remain fixed, while derivatives w.r.t. the action trajectory are retained.

D.1 Reduced-Space Optimization

We implement Equation 5 in standardized action coordinates. The action trajectory AA is the only optimization variable, with Z⁡(A)=ℛθ​(zt,A)Z(A)=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A). We solve

A⋆=arg​minA∈𝒰stdH⁡J​(Z⁡(A),g)+λA​dA​(A,A~)+λZ​dZ​(Z⁡(A),Z~),Z⋆=Z⁡(A⋆),A^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{A\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{std}}^{H}}J(Z(A),g)+\lambda_{A}d_{A}(A,\tilde{A})+\lambda_{Z}d_{Z}(Z(A),\tilde{Z}),\qquad Z^{\star}=Z(A^{\star}), (39)

where 𝒰std\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{std}} denotes the action bounds in standardized coordinates. The optimized future Z⋆Z^{\star} is always produced by the world model.

We use

J⁡(Z⁡(A),g)=‖ZH​(A)−g‖22,J(Z(A),g)=\|Z_{H}(A)-g\|_{2}^{2}, (40)

and

dA​(A,A~)=1H​∑h=0H−1‖Ah−A~h‖22,dZ​(Z,Z~)=1H​∑h=1H‖𝒩Z​(zh)−𝒩Z​(z~h)‖22.d_{A}(A,\tilde{A})=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\|A_{h}-\tilde{A}_{h}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad d_{Z}(Z,\tilde{Z})=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\|\mathcal{N}_{Z}(z_{h})-\mathcal{N}_{Z}(\tilde{z}_{h})\|_{2}^{2}. (41)

Primitive actions are standardized using offline-data statistics before forming action blocks. Environment action bounds are transformed with the same statistics and imposed as box constraints. The action reference A~\tilde{A} uses the same coordinates.

The state normalization is 𝒩Z​(z)=(z−μZ)/σZ\mathcal{N}_{Z}(z)=(z-\mu_{Z})/\sigma_{Z}, where μZ\mu_{Z} and σZ\sigma_{Z} are computed only from frozen-LeWM latents in the offline training split. This normalization is used only in dZd_{Z}; the task cost is evaluated in the native pretrained latent space. We use λA=10\lambda_{A}=10 and λZ=0.1\lambda_{Z}=0.1 in all experiments.

D.2 Numerical Solver

We initialize the primal solve from the clipped generated action reference A~\tilde{A}. We run L-BFGS-B for at most 200200 iterations under the standardized action bounds, followed by up to 2525 projected-gradient polishing iterations. Each polishing iteration uses at most 1212 backtracking trials.

Because the world model rollout is nonlinear, the optimization problem is generally nonconvex. We require local stationarity using

‖∇projΨ​(A⋆,A~,r~)‖∞≤0.02,\left\|\nabla_{\mathrm{proj}}\Psi(A^{\star};\tilde{A},\tilde{r})\right\|_{\infty}\leq 0.02, (42)

where the projected gradient is taken with respect to the standardized action bounds.

During training, a task sample whose solution fails Equation 42 is rejected and retried with another reserved window and proposal. We allow at most four attempts per update. If none satisfies the stationarity criterion, the task update is aborted.

The trajectory optimizer is used only during WATO training. Deployment uses generated proposals and world model evaluation without L-BFGS-B refinement.

D.3 Implicit Differentiation

We differentiate the local solution through its optimality conditions rather than unrolling the primal solver. Let y=(A~,r~)y=(\tilde{A},\tilde{r}), where r~=vec⁡𝒩Z​(Z~)\tilde{r}=\operatorname{vec}\mathcal{N}_{Z}(\tilde{Z}), and let A⋆​(y)A^{\star}(y) denote a local solution. For an interior regular solution, ∇AΨ​(A⋆,y)=0\nabla_{A}\Psi(A^{\star};y)=0. Define 𝖧=∇A​A2​Ψ​(A⋆,y)\mathsf{H}=\nabla_{AA}^{2}\Psi(A^{\star};y) and 𝖡=∂y∇AΨ​(A⋆,y)\mathsf{B}=\partial_{y}\nabla_{A}\Psi(A^{\star};y). Differentiating the stationarity condition gives

𝖧​∂A⋆∂y+𝖡=0.\mathsf{H}\frac{\partial A^{\star}}{\partial y}+\mathsf{B}=0. (43)

We only need the vector-Jacobian product with the task loss. Let

gtask=∇AJ​(ℛθ​(zt,A),g)|A=A⋆.g_{\mathrm{task}}=\left.\nabla_{A}J(\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A),g)\right|_{A=A^{\star}}. (44)

Rather than forming 𝖧−1\mathsf{H}^{-1}, we solve

𝖧⊤​v=gtask,∇yJ​(Z⋆,g)=−𝖡⊤​v.\mathsf{H}^{\top}v=g_{\mathrm{task}},\qquad\nabla_{y}J(Z^{\star},g)=-\mathsf{B}^{\top}v. (45)

The resulting reference gradients are propagated through the joint generator to update ϕ\phi.

Let

JR=∂ℛθ​(zt,A)∂A|A=A⋆,J_{R}=\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},A)}{\partial A}\right|_{A=A^{\star}}, (46)

and let DZD_{Z} denote the block-diagonal linear map induced by 𝒩Z\mathcal{N}_{Z}. The standardized rollout Jacobian is S⋆=DZ​JRS_{\star}=D_{Z}J_{R}. The joint WAF directly outputs the normalized state reference r~\tilde{r}, with task gradient

∇A~J​(Z⋆,g)=2​λAH​v,∇r~J​(Z⋆,g)=2​λZH​DZ​JR​v.\nabla_{\tilde{A}}J(Z^{\star},g)=\frac{2\lambda_{A}}{H}v,\qquad\nabla_{\tilde{r}}J(Z^{\star},g)=\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}D_{Z}J_{R}v. (47)

In native latent coordinates,

∇Z~J​(Z⋆,g)=DZ⊤​∇r~J​(Z⋆,g)=2​λZH​DZ⊤​DZ​JR​v.\nabla_{\tilde{Z}}J(Z^{\star},g)=D_{Z}^{\top}\nabla_{\tilde{r}}J(Z^{\star},g)=\frac{2\lambda_{Z}}{H}D_{Z}^{\top}D_{Z}J_{R}v. (48)

Thus, the generated future receives a task gradient through its effect on the optimized actions even though it is not an independent optimization variable.

For a box-constrained solution with a locally fixed active set, we differentiate only through the free action coordinates. Let EfreeE_{\mathrm{free}} embed the free coordinates into the full action vector. The theoretical adjoint system is

(Efree⊤​𝖧​Efree)⊤​vfree=Efree⊤​gtask,v=Efree​vfree.\left(E_{\mathrm{free}}^{\top}\mathsf{H}E_{\mathrm{free}}\right)^{\top}v_{\mathrm{free}}=E_{\mathrm{free}}^{\top}g_{\mathrm{task}},\qquad v=E_{\mathrm{free}}v_{\mathrm{free}}. (49)

This local derivative does not cover points where the active set changes.

In implementation, we solve the damped system

(Efree⊤​𝖧​Efree+10−3​I)⊤​vfree=Efree⊤​gtask.\left(E_{\mathrm{free}}^{\top}\mathsf{H}E_{\mathrm{free}}+10^{-3}I\right)^{\top}v_{\mathrm{free}}=E_{\mathrm{free}}^{\top}g_{\mathrm{task}}. (50)

We compute Hessianvector products through the frozen world model and use conjugate gradients for at most 1616 iterations with tolerance 10−410^{-4}. If conjugate gradients fails, we fall back to a dense solve and, when needed, a pseudoinverse. Damping and finite solver tolerance make the backward pass an approximation to the local sensitivity.

The world model parameters θ\theta are never updated by this gradient. Derivatives through ℛθ\mathcal{R}_{\theta} with respect to the action trajectory are retained.

Appendix E World Model and WAF Implementation

We specify the pretrained world model, joint world-action generator, and WATO training procedure. The world model and joint WAF are trained before WATO. WATO updates only the generator parameters ϕ\phi and the world model parameters θ\theta remain fixed.

E.1 World Model

We use latent world models following LeWM (Maes et al., 2026). Each model consists of a visual encoder EθE_{\theta} and an action-conditioned predictor FθF_{\theta} trained jointly end-to-end. The encoder maps an observation to a latent state, while the predictor takes an action block AhA_{h} and a finite latent context 𝒞h\mathcal{C}_{h} and predicts the next latent state. Autoregressive prediction gives the rollout ℛθ\mathcal{R}_{\theta} defined in Equation 1.

The released LeWM architecture uses 224×224224\times 224 visual inputs, a ViT-Tiny encoder with patch size 1414, and a six-layer action-conditioned Transformer predictor. For released checkpoints, five primitive actions are grouped into each action block. The predictor uses a finite latent context whose length depends on the environment.

LeWM is trained with next-latent prediction and SIGReg. The prediction loss is

ℒpred=𝔼𝒟​[MSE⁡(z^h+1,zh+1)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\operatorname{MSE}\left(\hat{z}_{h+1},z_{h+1}\right)\right], (51)

and the full objective is ℒWM=ℒpred+λsig​ℒSIG\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WM}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sig}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIG}}. Following LeWM, we use 10241024 random projections for SIGReg and λsig=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{sig}}=0.1.

We use released LeWM checkpoints when available. For environments without one, we train the same LeWM architecture and objective from scratch. We retain the default temporal abstraction of five primitive actions per latent transition and a maximum context of three latent states. For models trained in this work, the training entry reports the optimizer step of the selected validation checkpoint. Table 5 summarizes the configurations.

For world models trained in this work, we use AdamW with a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, weight decay of 10−310^{-3}, and batch size 128128. We train for up to 1212 epochs (approximately 9292k optimizer updates) with a 1%1\% linear warmup followed by cosine decay to zero, and clip the global gradient norm to 1.01.0. We select the checkpoint with the lowest teacher-forced validation loss, defined as prediction MSE plus 0.090.09 times the SIGReg loss.

All world models are trained before WATO. During WATO, gradients through EθE_{\theta}, FθF_{\theta}, and ℛθ\mathcal{R}_{\theta} with respect to their inputs are retained, but θ\theta is never updated.

E.2 Joint World Action Flow

The joint WAF models X=(A,Z)X=(A,Z), where A=(A0,…,AH−1)A=(A_{0},\ldots,A_{H-1}) and Z=(z1,…,zH)Z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{H}), conditioned on the current and goal latents c=(zt,g)c=(z_{t},g). A single conditional flow generates the action and future-state trajectories jointly rather than autoregressively over the horizon.

The vector field vϕv_{\phi} is parameterized by a Transformer with model width 256256, 44 Transformer layers, 88 attention heads, feed-forward dimension 10241024, no dropout, and a 6464-dimensional flow-time embedding. Action and latent variables are projected to the common model width, processed jointly, and mapped back to their respective output spaces. The model has approximately 3.53.5M parameters.

Primitive actions are standardized before action blocks are formed. Future state targets are obtained by encoding dataset observations with the pretrained encoder. For each minibatch, we sample a horizon-HH trajectory window, form X=(A,Z)X=(A,Z), and train with the joint WAF objective in Equation 3. We use λWAF=1\lambda_{\mathrm{WAF}}=1, batch size 512512, and 50,00050{,}000 pretraining updates.

At generation time, Gaussian noise with the same structure as XX is integrated from flow time 00 to 11. We use Euler integration with NFE =8=8. All action and state variables are updated jointly at each flow step. Unless otherwise stated, deployment draws K=8K=8 independent candidates.

E.3 WATO Training

WATO fine-tunes the pretrained joint WAF using the objective in Equation 9. The flow matching term preserves trajectory imitation, while the task term differentiates through the trajectory-optimization layer. Only the WAF parameters ϕ\phi are updated. The world model remains fixed.

We use AdamW with a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, and a flow matching batch size of 6464 for 10,00010{,}000 WATO updates. The task term uses one projected trajectory per update with λtask=5×10−3\lambda_{\mathrm{task}}=5\times 10^{-3}. For each update, trajectories for the task term are generated with Euler integration using NFE =2=2 and passed through the trajectory projection in Equation 4. We draw up to four proposals to obtain a stationarity-qualified trajectory. Only solutions satisfying the criterion in Equation 42 contribute to the task gradient.

We clip the global generator gradient norm to 11. The learning rate uses a linear warmup over the first 100100 updates followed by cosine decay to zero. We select the final checkpoint using the minimum fixed-validation objective, ℒWAF+λtask​ℒtask\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WAF}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{task}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}.

E.4 Training Cost and Solver Statistics

WATO adds training-time computation because each task update solves a trajectory optimization problem and differentiates through its solution. Table 7 reports statistics from the full 10,00010{,}000-update PushT run. All wall-clock times are measured on a single NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell GPU.

WATO fine-tuning takes 5.825.82 hours, compared with 1.761.76 hours for joint WAF pretraining. The primal solver uses 9090 L-BFGS-B iterations on average, but the stationarity filter rarely rejects a solve: only 55 of 10,00510{,}005 attempts are rejected, and no training update is aborted. The additional computation is confined to training; deployment uses generation, world model evaluation, and best-of-KK selection without iterative trajectory refinement.

Appendix F Experimental Protocol

This section specifies goal construction, baseline training, environment-specific configurations, and compute measurement. Unless stated otherwise, all methods use the same offline data, evaluation goals, execution budget, and pretrained visual representation. Figure 5 shows representative observations from the seven evaluation environments.

F.1 Goal Construction and Evaluation

We evaluate local visual goal reaching from evaluation trajectories. For an initial observation oto_{t}, the goal is the observation ot+Lo_{t+L} from the same trajectory, with L=25L=25 environment steps. All evaluation episodes are nontrivial: the initial state never satisfies the goal criterion. Only pairs with at least LL remaining steps are used. This defines the same goal distribution across all methods.

Each episode has a 5050-step execution budget. A controller repeatedly observes the current image, conditions on the fixed goal image, executes its selected action segment, and replans until success or the budget is exhausted. All methods use the same environment-specific success criterion.

Success rate is the primary metric. We also report the final latent goal error ‖Eθ​(oT)−g‖2\|E_{\theta}(o_{T})-g\|_{2}, where oTo_{T} is the final observation. All results use 44 seeds and identical start-goal pairs across methods.

F.2 Baseline Training

All baselines are trained on the same offline dataset and goal distribution as WATO. Evaluation uses identical start-goal pairs and the same execution budget. All methods use the same pretrained LeWM encoder to separate control performance from representation quality. Each baseline otherwise keeps its original objective, goal-relabeling procedure, and training scheme.

Goal-conditioned learning.

GCBC (Ding et al., 2019) learns a goal-conditioned policy by behavioral cloning. GCIVL (Kostrikov et al., 2022) and GCIQL (Park et al., 2025a) learn goal-conditioned value functions and policies from the same offline data. QRL (Wang et al., 2023) learns goal-conditioned control through its quasimetric objective. All four methods are trained from scratch for this goal distribution rather than evaluated with published final-goal checkpoints.

Generative control.

The Flow policy generates only the action trajectory AA and serves as the action-only generative baseline. Joint WAF uses the joint generator qϕ(A,Z∣zt,g)q_{\phi}(A,Z\mid z_{t},g) trained only with the flow matching objective in Equation 3. It isolates the effect of WATO training from joint trajectory imitation. For GPC (Kurtz and Burdick, 2026), we adapt the method to the same offline setting and use the same pretrained LeWM dynamics model as WATO. All generative methods use the same goals and execution budget.

Model-based control.

CEM (Maes et al., 2026; Kim and Sreenath, 2026b) optimizes action trajectories online using the same pretrained world model and terminal task cost JJ as WATO. It uses a population of 300300 trajectories, retains 3030 elites (an elite fraction of 0.10.1), and performs 3030 optimization rounds for PushT and Reacher and 1010 rounds for the OGBench manipulation environments. The initial standard deviation is 11, no warm start is used, and the final Gaussian mean is returned as the action plan. Gradient-based MPC uses 88 independently initialized action trajectories, 4040 gradient steps, and a learning rate of 0.050.05. Neither method updates the world model during evaluation.

We use the released LeWM CEM hyperparameters without tuning. Hyperparameters for learned baselines are selected on validation tasks and then fixed for test evaluation.

F.3 Hyperparameters

We use the same WATO configuration across all environments. The planning horizon is H=5H=5 latent transitions with B=5B=5 primitive actions per block. At deployment, WATO generates K=8K=8 candidates using Euler integration with NFE =8=8. We set λA=10\lambda_{A}=10, λZ=0.1\lambda_{Z}=0.1, and λtask=5×10−3\lambda_{\mathrm{task}}=5\times 10^{-3}. The trajectory optimizer uses at most 200200 L-BFGS-B iterations during WATO training and is not used at deployment. Ablations change only the component specified by each experiment.

F.4 Success Criteria

We evaluate success using environment-specific semantic state criteria rather than the latent-space terminal cost used for planning. The latent cost ranks candidate action trajectories, while success is computed from simulator state. Table 8 summarizes the criterion for each environment.

An episode is successful if its criterion is satisfied at least once during execution. WATO and the other WAF-based controllers terminate immediately upon success. The released Reacher CEM parity evaluator is an exception: it continues until the full episode budget is exhausted but keeps the first observed success for evaluation.

Appendix G Full Results

This section reports the per-environment results underlying the aggregate comparisons in the main paper. We provide the full WATO ablations, the absolute success rates used to measure optimization amortization, and final goal errors.

G.1 Full WATO Ablations

Table 9 reports the complete training-objective and reference-design ablations. All variants use the same joint WAF architecture, offline data, pretrained world model, and evaluation protocol.

The training-objective ablation isolates how trajectory optimization enters learning. Joint WAF uses flow matching alone. Direct rollout adds task supervision through the world model, direct rollout with consistency additionally aligns generated states with the rollout, and distillation uses optimized trajectories as detached targets. WATO achieves the highest average success rate, improving from 79.9%79.9\% for Joint WAF to 91.7%91.7\%.

The reference-design ablation isolates the two components of the world-action trajectory. Using only the action reference achieves 85.7%85.7\%, while using only the state reference achieves 85.0%85.0\%. Their combination reaches 91.7%91.7\%, showing that neither reference alone recovers full WATO performance.

Removing dZd_{Z} eliminates both its dynamics-aware regularization and the generated future reference. To separate these effects, the rollout-derived variant replaces Z~\tilde{Z} with ℛθ​(zt,A~)\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(z_{t},\tilde{A}) while retaining both reference penalties. The backward pass includes the dependence of this reference on A~\tilde{A}. This retains dynamics-aware regularization without using the generated future as a control reference, as discussed in Appendix C.2.

The average success rate of 87.9%87.9\% place this variant 2.22.2 pp above the action-reference-only variant and 3.83.8 points below WATO. This indicate that dynamics-aware regularization explains part, but not all, of the state-reference benefit. The remaining gap support using generated futures to guide optimization beyond the consequences already predicted for the proposed actions. Conversely, performance comparable to WATO suggest that rollout-derived references capture most of this benefit.

G.2 Training Horizon and Test Goal Distance

The main experiments use a training horizon Ltrain=25L_{\mathrm{train}}=25 and test goals D=25D=25 primitive steps ahead. We additionally vary Ltrain∈{10,25,50,100}L_{\mathrm{train}}\in\{10,25,50,100\} and D∈{10,25,50,100}D\in\{10,25,50,100\} on PushT, cube-single, and scene-play. For each goal distance DD, the execution budget is 2​D2D steps. All other settings are unchanged.

These horizons correspond to physical durations. In PushT, one environment step is 0.10.1 s, so Ltrain={10,25,50,100}L_{\mathrm{train}}=\{10,25,50,100\} corresponds to {1,2.5,5,10}\{1,2.5,5,10\} s. In cube-single and scene-play, one step is 0.050.05 s, giving {0.5,1.25,2.5,5}\{0.5,1.25,2.5,5\} s. The execution budget is twice the test-goal duration.

Table 10 shows that WATO is not limited to short local control. The best training horizon generally grows with the test goal distance, although exact matching is not always optimal. For example, Ltrain=50L_{\mathrm{train}}=50 achieves 82%82\% success on PushT at D=50D=50, corresponding to a 55 s trajectory. An average PushT episode spans roughly 125125 steps, or 12.512.5 s, so a 5050-step WATO horizon already covers about 40%40\% of a full episode. A complete task therefore spans only about two to three such horizons, leaving less work for a separate high-level planner than a purely local-controller view would suggest.

Performance still decreases as the temporal scale grows. At D=100D=100, the best success rates are 48%48\%, 58%58\%, and 52%52\% on PushT, cube-single, and scene-play, respectively. Longer tasks with more objects, stages, or distant goals may therefore benefit from hierarchy or high-level planning. Such a planner, however, can operate over multi-second WATO controllers rather than primitive local actions. These results further support the perspective in Appendix B: WATO is a strong default controller over a broader temporal range than the main 2525-step setting alone suggests.

G.3 Full Optimization-Amortization Results

The main paper reports the additional success obtained by applying trajectory optimization before and after WATO training. Table 11 reports the corresponding absolute success rates.

Before WATO, trajectory optimization raises average success from 79.9%79.9\% to 90.3%90.3\%. After WATO, the same optimizer raises success only from 91.7%91.7\% to 93.0%93.0\%. Thus, most of the performance previously obtained through online optimization is already present in the WATO generator.

The absolute results also separate optimization quality from amortization. Online trajectory optimization is already strong when applied to the imitation-trained generator, reaching 90.3%90.3\% average success. WATO reaches 91.7%91.7\% without this online optimization, while an additional optimization step provides only a small remaining gain. This supports the interpretation that WATO transfers the useful effect of trajectory optimization into generation rather than relying on a weak optimizer.

G.4 Final Goal Error

Success is a thresholded measure and does not distinguish failures that terminate near the goal from those that remain far away. We therefore also report the final latent goal error ‖Eθ​(oT)−g‖2\|E_{\theta}(o_{T})-g\|_{2}, where oTo_{T} is the final observation after the execution budget. Lower values indicate trajectories that terminate closer to the target.

Table 12 reports the metric for the same methods and start-goal pairs as Table 1. We report results separately for each environment because latent scales need not be comparable across independently trained world models.

Final goal error complements success rate but does not replace it. Success remains the primary metric because the evaluation criterion is defined in the environment, while latent distance measures how closely the final observation matches the goal under the shared representation.

Appendix H Deployment Efficiency Details

This section expands the deployment-efficiency comparison in Sec. 5.8. We report per-environment latency, define the world model computation count, and study the effect of WATO sampling budget on success and deployment cost.

H.1 Per-Environment Latency

We measure the wall-clock cost of one planning step. WATO includes joint trajectory generation, world model evaluation of all generated action candidates, candidate selection, and action extraction. CEM includes all online optimization iterations and world model rollouts.

Table 13 reports absolute deployment latency in seconds. The corresponding relative speedups are reported in Table 3. Absolute latency varies across environments, so we report per-environment values rather than averaging raw times.

H.2 World Model Evaluations

Wall-clock latency depends on hardware and batching, so we also report world model computation directly. We count one world model evaluation as one latent transition Fθ​(𝒞h,Ah)F_{\theta}(\mathcal{C}_{h},A_{h}) for one candidate trajectory. A full horizon-HH rollout therefore uses HH evaluations.

WATO generates KK action candidates and rolls each candidate through the world model once. Its cost per planning step is therefore

NWMWATO=K​H.N_{\mathrm{WM}}^{\mathrm{WATO}}=KH. (52)

The flow matching-only joint WAF uses the same deployment procedure and therefore has the same world model count,

NWMJoint​WAF=K​H.N_{\mathrm{WM}}^{\mathrm{Joint\ WAF}}=KH. (53)

Let NCEMN_{\mathrm{CEM}} denote the number of CEM iterations and MCEMM_{\mathrm{CEM}} the population size. Each iteration evaluates all candidates over the full horizon, giving

NWMCEM=NCEM​MCEM​H.N_{\mathrm{WM}}^{\mathrm{CEM}}=N_{\mathrm{CEM}}M_{\mathrm{CEM}}H. (54)

For gradient-based MPC, let NgradN_{\mathrm{grad}} be the number of optimization steps and MinitM_{\mathrm{init}} the number of parallel initial action trajectories. Each optimization step requires a forward rollout through the horizon, so

NWMGrad.MPC=Ngrad​Minit​H.N_{\mathrm{WM}}^{\mathrm{Grad.\ MPC}}=N_{\mathrm{grad}}M_{\mathrm{init}}H. (55)

Backward differentiation is included in wall-clock latency but not counted as an additional forward world model evaluation.

Because all compared methods use the same horizon HH, the relative forward-model cost is independent of HH. For example, the CEM-to-WATO ratio is

NWMCEMNWMWATO=NCEM​MCEMK.\frac{N_{\mathrm{WM}}^{\mathrm{CEM}}}{N_{\mathrm{WM}}^{\mathrm{WATO}}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{CEM}}M_{\mathrm{CEM}}}{K}. (56)

This count is independent of batching: evaluating KK candidates in one batched forward pass still counts as K​HKH latent transitions.

H.3 Success-Compute Tradeoff

WATO exposes two deployment-time compute parameters. The candidate count KK controls how many generated action trajectories are evaluated by the world model, while NFE controls the cost of flow integration. Increasing either can improve candidate quality or coverage at additional compute.

We evaluate K∈{1,4,8,16}K\in\{1,4,8,16\} with NFE fixed at 88, and NFE∈{4,8,16}\mathrm{NFE}\in\{4,8,16\} with KK fixed at 88. All other settings remain unchanged. Figure 6 reports average success across the 77 environments against deployment latency, with the number of world model evaluations shown for each setting.

Increasing KK gives a clear gain from one to eight candidates, while the improvement from K=8K=8 to K=16K=16 is small despite the additional world model evaluations and latency. Increasing NFE shows a similar pattern: NFE =8=8 captures most of the gain, with little improvement from doubling the integration steps to 1616. We therefore use K=8K=8 and NFE =8=8 as the default, which lies near the knee of both tradeoffs.

Appendix I Call for Research

WATO leaves further questions: what should we learn to do quickly, and what should we still plan online? A strong local controller lets us ask where reasoning, value learning, and additional computation are actually most useful.

A strong controller is only the beginning.

Long-horizon goal reaching has benefited from hierarchical learning (Park et al., 2023; Park et al., 2025a; Kim et al., 2025), but reliably composing local behaviors from offline visual data remains open. Reaching waypoints is not enough if the resulting state makes the next transition difficult. A high-level plan must choose reachable goals, leave the controller in useful states, and recover when execution deviates from the plan. This is more than simply increasing the horizon. We need work that local execution, subgoal selection, and their composition.

World action models beyond scale.

WAM research need not be only about building larger foundation models. As discussed in Appendix A, joint WAMs also form a generative control model class whose objectives, references, and deployment rules deserve study. How should generated futures influence actions? When does joint generation help beyond an equally expressive action-only policy? Which control principles transfer across architectures and scales? Large-scale pretraining and control optimization address different questions. Better generation and better control need not come from the same design choices.

Put values and broad knowledge where they help most.

Our results also raise a question about where value learning belongs. If local trajectories can already be generated reliably, values may be more useful for selecting subgoals and stitching behaviors than for extracting every motor action. Hierarchical goal-conditioned learning provides a natural starting point (Park et al., 2023). High-level values should also reflect what the deployed low-level controller can actually execute, including its failures, rather than only what transitions appear in the dataset.

Large foundation models may similarly be most useful for semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and goal selection, while a dynamics-aware controller handles local execution. SayCan illustrates how broad knowledge can be grounded through executable skills and their values (Ahn et al., 2022). At the same time, pretrained WAMs can directly generate low-level control (Ye et al., 2026). The question is therefore not only how much to scale, but where to put that scale.

Act fast, deliberate when needed.

Thinking fast and slow (Kahneman et al., 2011) suggests allocating computation according to the decision. A familiar subgoal may need only one forward pass, while difficult contact may justify extra sampling or optimization. A useful extension of WATO would decide when direct generation is enough and when to refine a trajectory, increase sampling, or reconsider the goal. Progress, uncertainty, or disagreement between generated and predicted futures could provide such signals, but they should be validated against execution outcomes. The goal is to spend extra computation when it actually improves control.

Will more compute solve planning, or exploit model error?

Faster hardware, GPU parallelism, and better solvers may make online trajectory optimization attractive. Systems such as cuRobo already show large gains from parallel optimization (Sundaralingam et al., 2023). CEM is also not simply brute-force search: variants such as iCEM use temporal correlations and memory to improve sampling efficiency (Pinneri et al., 2020). Future planners may further use learned proposals or references, erasing the distinction between online optimization and learned generation.

The harder question is whether computation or model error becomes the bottleneck. More search can reduce predicted cost without making the world model more accurate, and may even find trajectories that exploit prediction errors (Yu et al., 2020; Kim and Sreenath, 2026a). WATO’s imitation loss and generated references guide optimization, but they do not guarantee model accuracy either. A generator can also learn model exploitation. Optimization error and model error therefore matter for both online planning and amortized control, as reflected in Appendix C.4.

For local visual goals, WATO should be your favorite controller. The next challenges are: where to go ∙\;\bullet\; when to think harder ∙\;\bullet\; how to leverage local abilities in a long horizon.
